name: Peacock Blue
lede: Peacock blue is the greenish blue of a peacock, a name Paterson defines as greenish blue and one that turns up in Victorian fashion pairings.

sections.title: A bird's neck
sections.body: Paterson defines *peacock blue* as a greenish blue and lists *peacock green* ([[green]]) beside it [1]. The color sits between [[blue]], [[teal]] and [[turquoise]], saturated and a little darker than the last [1][2].

sections.title: Peacock cloths
sections.body: Pastoureau mentions *panni pavonacei*, "peacock" cloths in a rich blue made from high-quality Thuringian woad, among luxury cloths that German cities prohibited under sumptuary laws [2][3]. The concern, he says, was the costly dye rather than the color itself [2][3]. In Italy the laws he names target the red Venetian scarlets [2][3]. The Italian word *pavonazzo*, which Paterson defines as peacock-coloured, greenish blue, is a related term [1].

sections.title: A fashionable partner
sections.body: St Clair's chapter on purple notes that in the late nineteenth century a heliotrope shade was paired with light green, apricot, canary yellow, eucalyptus green, art bronze and peacock blue [4]. One commentator of the time said the combinations were sometimes startling [4].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: The swatch here is #026998, a deep, saturated blue with a trace of green [5]. As with all dictionary colors, a feather's iridescence changes with the viewing angle, so no single screen value can match it [1][5].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: This is a rare color in paintings: 30 of 23,781 canvases in the ColorHub archive hold it across at least 5% of the picture, as photographed [5]. The match rate is about three times the average in the 1880s, and Impressionist pictures show it at roughly eleven times the average, though from only 2 canvases [5]. The earliest match is from 1482 [5].

origin.first_recorded: origin undocumented in the books; panni pavonacei in sumptuary-law discussions (Pastoureau, undated)
